indicators.note: something repaired has been put back together, so these letters are reassembled

explanation.surface: A robot's right boot has been mended.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Automaton's' is read as 'Automaton is', so the possessive is a link to the wordplay; 'repaired' is the anagram signal on the boot.
explanation.definitionFit: A mechanical figure that performs actions by itself is a machine of this kind.

clue.text: One might have set features at work

definitions.text: One might have set features at work

parts.words: One might have set features at work
parts.note: features here are newspaper articles, and the person at work deciding which go in the paper sets them

explanation.definitionFit: A newspaper's senior journalist chooses and arranges the feature articles.

clue.text: Careless loose arm could be dangerous in it, but lots go there

indicators.note: careless handling throws these words into disorder, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Waving an arm about at an auction can land you a purchase, since that is where the lots are sold.
explanation.walkthrough: A careless arm movement at an auction may be taken as a bid, which is why it 'could be dangerous in it'. 'Careless' rearranges LOOSE ARM.
explanation.definitionFit: Auction lots are offered for sale in a dedicated room where bidders gather.

clue.text: Waggoner reverses with little time to spare — has to pull back

indicators.note: the waggoner is said to reverse, which tells us to read his name backwards

parts.note: a waggoner drives a cart, so he is a carter
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A cart driver backs his wagon with seconds to spare as he must withdraw.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reverses' looks like the waggoner backing his cart, but it tells you to write his trade backwards before the little time is tacked on.
explanation.definitionFit: To withdraw a claim or draw something in is to take it back.

parts.note: John Peel is the huntsman of the old song who rose early in the morning with his hounds; his people are of the same trade

explanation.walkthrough: 'Peel' suggests Robert Peel and his police, but the song 'D'ye ken John Peel' is about a Cumbrian huntsman out 'in the morning'.
explanation.definitionFit: Men who ride to hounds, chasing foxes, rise at dawn for the hunt.

parts.note: P is the abbreviation for a penny, so two of them make PP

explanation.surface: A tax assessor points out that the rates have gone up by tuppence, which is fair.
explanation.walkthrough: P stands for a penny in British money, so twopence gives PP.
explanation.definitionFit: A valuer who sets the worth of property, for tax or sale, assesses it.

definitions.meaning: printing type with heavy thick letters

explanation.definitionFit: Shameless and cheeky in manner; also, heavy thick printing letters used for emphasis.

definitions.meaning: forces out in jets, as a heart does blood
lightweight shoes such as dancing slippers or plimsolls

explanation.surface: Bursts of speed in lightweight footwear.
explanation.definitionFit: Drives liquid out in bursts; also slip-on lightweight footwear for dancing or sport.

clue.text: Flying Iron Cross holder has a way of banking

indicators.note: the phrase holds letters that cross from one word into the next, so the answer sits inside it

explanation.surface: A German pilot decorated with the Iron Cross banks his plane in flight.
explanation.walkthrough: The run is in flyinG IROn, crossing the word gap. 'Banking' suggests an aircraft turning, but it is the money sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A system of transferring money directly between bank or post-office accounts.

parts.note: a radical goes to the root of things, so his draught or drink is named after roots

explanation.walkthrough: A radical, from Latin radix, goes to the root; the drink is flavoured with root extracts.
explanation.definitionFit: A fizzy soft drink flavoured with sassafras and other plant extracts.

parts.note: to bury a body is to inter it

explanation.surface: A pupil boards at school in the Lancashire town of Bury in the North.
explanation.walkthrough: Bury is a town near Manchester in northern England, which makes 'Bury (North)' look like a place.
explanation.definitionFit: A pupil who lives in at a school, a boarder, is resident there.

indicators.note: a word left unopened has lost its first letter

explanation.surface: The goods are still sealed in the hold of Jason's vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unopened' drops the first letter of CARGO.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek legend the Argonauts sailed in this vessel to fetch the Golden Fleece.

clue.text: How mince is cooked in Chinese restaurants

definitions.text: How mince is cooked in Chinese restaurants

indicators.note: cooking the words, like cooking the books, mixes their letters into a new order

explanation.surface: A question of how minced meat is prepared in Chinese restaurants.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition and the wordplay: 'is cooked' rearranges HOW MINCE into a dish served in Chinese restaurants.
explanation.definitionFit: A Chinese-style dish of fried noodles with shredded meat and vegetables.

parts.note: the seven dwarfs work in a mine in Disney's cartoon, and the heroine who lives with them could be called their leader

explanation.walkthrough: 'Animated' looks like 'lively', and 'miners' leader' like a trade-union boss, but it is the 1937 Disney cartoon.
explanation.definitionFit: The fairy-tale princess who keeps house for the seven dwarfs, star of Disney's first feature cartoon.

clue.text: Physical structure of a toy man, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps says the letters given could be something else, here rearranged

explanation.surface: The bodily build of a toy figure, maybe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges A TOY MAN.
explanation.definitionFit: The bodily make-up of a living thing, studied by doctors.

clue.text: Injunction to raconteur could be revealing

definitions.meaning: an order to a storyteller to recount his story
giving away something hidden, as a sign does

explanation.surface: Asking a storyteller to go on may give something away.
explanation.definitionFit: An order to a storyteller to recount his story; also, giving away a secret, as a betraying sign does.

parts.note: striking reads as hitting, so this is someone who smacks others

explanation.walkthrough: 'Striking' looks like 'impressive' and the word does mean a fine specimen, but it is also one who smacks.
explanation.definitionFit: One who smacks a child's bottom; also a fine example of anything, and a sail on a ship.

clue.text: Common leg with head of goose has bad smell as game for table

parts.note: pins is common or everyday slang for legs

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: pong is British slang for a stink

explanation.surface: An ordinary leg plus a goose's head smells awful, a dish for the table.
explanation.walkthrough: PONG is British slang for a bad smell.
explanation.definitionFit: Table tennis is played with bats and a light ball over a net on a table.

clue.text: Church in utter collapse here in the Netherlands

indicators.note: the church is placed in the jumbled letters
something that collapses falls to bits, so the letters are reshuffled

explanation.surface: A church in a state of complete ruin somewhere in Holland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'collapse' turns UTTER into UTRET, and CH goes 'in' it.
explanation.definitionFit: A Dutch city and province, site of an early-18th-century peace treaty.

definitions.meaning: in Wagner's music the gods have their Gotterdammerung, the dusk of the gods

explanation.walkthrough: 'Notedly' means in music: Wagner's opera Gotterdammerung is usually rendered as the Twilight of the Gods.
explanation.definitionFit: Dusk, the dim light after sunset; also the doom of the gods in Wagner's last Ring opera.

definitions.meaning: spare or surplus, in naval slang

explanation.definitionFit: Spare or superfluous in British slang; also a long deep wound.

indicators.note: section of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A dainty part of a classical Ionic doorway.
explanation.definitionFit: Fine or subtle, as a nice distinction is a finely drawn one.

clue.text: Providers of effective treatment for smokers, perhaps

definitions.meaning: people who preserve fish or ham by smoking it

explanation.surface: Healers offering a remedy for those who smoke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For smokers' suggests a way to stop smoking, but smokers are people who smoke fish or bacon to preserve it.
explanation.definitionFit: Healers who make patients well; also those who preserve meat or fish by salting or smoking.

clue.text: Overbearing fellow to start hockey match

definitions.meaning: in field hockey, the ...-off is how play once began

explanation.surface: A domineering type is chosen to get the hockey game under way.
explanation.definitionFit: A tormentor of the weak; also, in field hockey, the face-off that once began play.

indicators.note: off means out of order or wrong, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone tells a cricketer to show off his kit, in old spelling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' rearranges SHEW IT ('shew' is an old spelling of 'show'). Cricketers traditionally play in white flannels.
explanation.definitionFit: Cricketers' traditional pale flannel clothing, named for its colour.

clue.text: Great store providing revised premium with nothing added

indicators.note: the nothing is added within the rearranged letters
revised means altered, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: nothing is zero, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A large shop offers a revised premium with nothing extra charged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revised' turns PREMIUM into EMPRIUM, and O is 'added' inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A large shop selling many kinds of goods, a department store.

clue.text: Place to work in mine or sit in pit

definitions.meaning: a working space at a coal face
a seat in the ... of a theatre, once called the pit

explanation.surface: Somewhere to work underground, or a seat in the pit.
explanation.walkthrough: In a theatre the pit was the floor seating, now the stalls; in a coal mine a stall is a working area at the coal face.
explanation.definitionFit: A working space at a coal face; also a theatre seat on the ground floor.

parts.note: James Hilton's novel Lost Horizon describes an ideal valley high in the Himalayas

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hilton' suggests the hotel chain, but James Hilton wrote Lost Horizon (1933) about a hidden paradise in Tibet.
explanation.definitionFit: An imaginary earthly paradise in a remote Himalayan valley.
